opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think it's an either-or question. You really need both, and they solve different problems.

Before deployment is where you do the heavy lifting that's expensive to figure out but cheap to reuse. Think quantization choices, kernel selection and fusion, choosing the right parallelism strategy across GPUs, compiling the model graph for the specific hardware you're targeting. Those decisions depend on the model architecture and the hardware, and they don't change request to request. So you want to search that space offline, carefully, with real quality evaluation. You don't want to be guessing at quantization in production and finding out later that you degraded accuracy on some long-tail task your customer cares about.

But a lot of what determines real-world performance only shows up at runtime. The traffic pattern, the mix of prompt lengths versus generation lengths, how bursty the load is, whether many requests share a common prefix so you get high cache hit rates. Those things vary by customer and even by hour of the day. So at runtime you're doing things like continuous batching, KV cache management and prefix caching, speculative decoding where the acceptance rate depends heavily on the actual workload, and routing and autoscaling decisions. A configuration that's optimal for a chatbot with short turns can be pretty bad for a RAG workload with huge contexts or an agentic workload making many sequential calls.

The way we think about it is that there's no one-size-fits-all optimal configuration. Latency, throughput, cost, and quality form a multi-dimensional tradeoff, and every application wants a different point in that space. So the offline work narrows the space to a good set of candidates, and then the runtime system, informed by actual production traffic, picks and adapts within that space. Increasingly we're also closing the loop: what you observe at runtime feeds back into the offline stage, whether that means retuning the draft model for speculative decoding on the customer's real data or picking a different quantization or sharding setup because the workload turned out to be different from what everyone assumed.

The mistake I see most often is teams optimizing against a synthetic benchmark before deployment and calling it done. The benchmark numbers look great, and then production traffic looks nothing like the benchmark. So my advice is to do your static optimizations rigorously, and also build the system so it can keep adapting once it meets real users.

r001.rationale: The response describes using both offline and runtime optimization, and mentions compiling the model graph before deployment, but it does not compare that combination to JIT and AOT compilation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and honestly it's one we think about constantly at Fireworks, because the answer is really "both," but they solve very different problems.

Let me start with the pre-deployment side, because I think that's where a lot of the biggest wins are, and it's also where people underinvest. When you're preparing a model for production, you have a huge amount of leverage. You know the model architecture, you can do quantization—FP8, INT8, in some cases even lower precision—you can compile and fuse kernels, you can tune for the specific hardware you're going to run on, whether that's H100s or MI300s or whatever. You can profile the workload offline and pick the right parallelism strategy, tensor parallel versus pipeline parallel, decide how you want to shard the KV cache, all of those things. None of that is cheap to do, but you only pay the cost once, and then every single request benefits. So my philosophy is: anything that can be decided ahead of time should be decided ahead of time. Don't make the runtime do work that you could have done at build time.

But here's the thing—you can't decide everything ahead of time, because the workload isn't static. That's the part that I think people coming from traditional ML systems sometimes underestimate with generative AI. With a classic recommendation model or a vision classifier, the input shapes are fixed, the compute per request is fixed, you can basically pre-plan everything. With LLMs, every request is different. Prompt lengths vary by orders of magnitude. Generation lengths are unknown when you start—you don't know if the model is going to produce ten tokens or two thousand. Traffic patterns shift during the day. Some users are hammering you with long-context RAG prompts and others are doing short chat turns. So there's this whole class of decisions that have to happen at runtime: how you batch, continuous batching, how you schedule prefill versus decode, how you manage the KV cache under memory pressure, when you evict, whether to do prefix caching and how much to reuse, whether speculative decoding is actually helping for this particular traffic mix or hurting it. Those are inherently dynamic.

So the way I frame it internally is kind of like a compiler versus an operating system. The compiler does the heavy static optimization, gets you a really efficient artifact. The operating system handles the dynamic scheduling and resource management because it's the only thing that can see the actual load. You need both, and a really good inference stack is one where those two layers are designed together, so the runtime has enough knobs exposed from the pre-deployment stage to adapt well.

And one more thing I'd add—there's actually a feedback loop between the two. A lot of what we learn at runtime, looking at real production traffic, feeds back into what we optimize ahead of time. If we see that a customer's traffic is ninety percent short prompts with a lot of shared prefixes, that changes how we'd want to quantize, how we'd lay out the cache, maybe even whether we'd recommend fine-tuning a smaller model. So I don't think of it as a one-time choice between runtime and pre-deployment. It's more of a continuous cycle where production observations keep refining the offline optimization.

r001.rationale: The response compares pre-deployment optimization to a compiler and runtime optimization to an operating system, but does not liken their combination to JIT and AOT compilation.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a combination of both. Before deployment, you can do a lot of optimization because you know the model and the hardware you’re targeting. You can optimize the computation graph, fuse operators, and choose numerical precision that gives you the performance you need while preserving quality. That gives you a strong baseline.

But you don’t know everything ahead of time. At runtime, requests arrive at different rates, input lengths vary, and the resources available can change. So decisions like batching, scheduling, and managing memory need to adapt to what’s actually happening.

The way I think about it is: do the work ahead of time when the information is stable, and leave the decisions that depend on live traffic to runtime. Those two layers need to work together, guided by the latency, throughput, and cost requirements of the application.

r001.rationale: The response describes combining predeployment and runtime optimization, but it does not compare that combination to JIT and AOT compilation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of those as complementary. Before deployment, you can do a lot because you know the model: optimize the graph, fuse operators, choose precision, and tune kernels for the target hardware. That gives you a strong baseline without adding work to each request.

But you don’t know everything ahead of time. At runtime, the batch size, sequence lengths, traffic patterns, and available memory can change. So you also need decisions about batching, scheduling, and memory management that respond to the actual workload.

The question is really: what can you decide ahead of time, and what depends on information you only have at runtime? Do the predictable work before deployment, then keep enough flexibility at runtime to meet your latency and throughput goals.

r001.rationale: The response describes predeployment and runtime optimization as complementary, but it does not compare that combination to JIT and AOT compilation.
